For this Physics-II paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Hand-checked: ⁴⁰Ca has Z = 20 and N = 40 − 20 = 20; ³⁹K has Z = 19 and N = 39 − 19 = 20, so the two are isotones. ⁸⁰Brᵐ and ⁸⁰Brᵍ share Z = 35 and A = 80 and differ only in nuclear energy state, so they are isomers.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Isotones
steps.mark_note: Same N, different Z, with example
lines: Isotones: nuclei with the same neutron
number N but different atomic numbers Z

lines.text: Ex: ⁴⁰Ca and ³⁹K, both with N = A − Z = 20.

steps.margin_note: First mark. Same N and different Z, plus one named example.
steps.why: N counts only the neutrons, so isotones are different elements that happen to hold the same number of neutrons.
common_mistakes: Writing "same mass number" — that is isobars, not isotones.
Giving no example. The pair ⁴⁰Ca and ³⁹K carries part of the credit.

recall.must_convey: That isotones have the same neutron number N but different atomic numbers Z, with an example such as calcium-40 and potassium-39.
accept: same neutron number different atomic number
calcium forty and potassium thirty nine
reject: same atomic number and same mass number

steps.memory_tip: isotoNe — the N says same Neutron number.

steps.label: Isomers
steps.mark_note: Same Z and same A, different nuclear state
lines: Isomers: nuclei with the same atomic number
Z and the same mass number A but different

lines.text: Ex: ⁸⁰Brᵐ and ⁸⁰Brᵍ are isomers.
Isotones: same N · Isomers: same Z and A

steps.margin_note: Second mark. Same Z AND same A; only the nuclear state differs.
steps.why: The two isomers are the same nucleus at two different energy levels: the m form sits in a long-lived excited state and reaches the ground state g by emitting a γ ray, so the half-lives differ.
common_mistakes: Saying isomers are different elements. They are the same nucleus in two states.
Confusing isomers with isotopes. Isotopes differ in A; isomers do not.

recall.must_convey: That isomers have the same atomic number Z and the same mass number A but different nuclear properties, with an example such as the two forms of bromine-80.
accept: same Z and same A but different nuclear properties
same nucleus in two energy states

steps.memory_tip: Isomer: everything on the label is the same, only the inside energy differs.

insider_note: Both halves need the defining pair of numbers AND one named example; a definition with no example loses part of the mark.
